en: The Cūrṇikā Explaining the Twenty-Four Names Composed by Śrī Bhadrācalarāmadāsa.

The ten directions [are illuminated] by the intensely radiant mandala of the staffs and sub-staffs of the glorious vessel of all millions of cosmic eggs— the Supreme beyond the qualified and the unqualified, the Transcendent, the Savior known as Brahman, who is Existence-Consciousness-Bliss.
To the radiant Śrī Mukunda, the sovereign of all that is moving and unmoving,
whose blazing divine lotus feet are being worshipped by the entire host of deities headed by Brahmā and Indra.

To the illustrious Raghuvīra, whose various incarnations are adorned with the conduct of a master playwright of the drama of deceit— intense in his suppression of the wicked and protection of the virtuous—
and who has blossomed as the fulfillment of the desires of Kausalyā and Daśaratha.
To Śrī Keśava, whose childhood was characterized by the playful tossing of wrestling matches;

to the glorious Nārāyaṇa, who is the ultimate consummation of skill in archery, having crushed the strength of the arms of Subāhu— who acted as the formidable Tāṭakā and caused obstacles for Viśvāmitra.
To Śrī Mādhava— the Lord of the Earth praised by Gautama and Satī, who were transformed by a curse into the form of stones to be touched by the thick waters of His own lotus feet; [and] who,
with His belly, broke the fierce bow that was raised to shatter [the world].

To Śrī Govinda, who brought joy to the eyes of Kauśika through the divine rod [of punishment], who was the delight of Janaka, the lord of the Cakras, and the bliss of the wedding festival of Sītā offered by him;
and who shattered the pride and arrogance of Paraśurāma’s arms.
To the illustrious Viṣṇu—who brings about the quenching [of worldly existence], who is followed by those who have crossed over the ocean of saṃsāra, who is victorious, and who is ever-increasing;

who, out of intense devotion to fulfilling his father’s word, was accompanied by Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa while wearing matted hair and bark garments; who was honored by the desire for sovereignty, yet whose firm vow impelled him toward his departure.
The *Raṅga-gaṅgāvataraṇa-sādhana* by Śrī Madhusūdana;
and the *Bharadvājopacāra-nivārita-mārgaśrama-nirāghāṭa-citrakūṭa-praveśakrama* by Śrī Trivikrama.

To the venerable Vāmana, who— by the command of Janaka, amidst the grief-stricken Bharata and Śatrughna, in accordance with the wishes of his beloved wife, and through the offering of his sandals— subdued the pride of the cruel demon Kāka, who was manifesting wicked intentions within Sītā’s heart.
To Śrī Śrīdhara, who is like a rain-cloud for the fire-flames of Virāṭa’s wrath that obstructed the journey to Daṇḍaka,
and who is the sincere bestower of blessings upon the sight of Śarabhaṅga, Sutīkṣṇa, and Atri.
The illustrious Hṛṣīkeśa, born from a pitcher, obtained through compassion, resplendent and honored by a multitude of great divine weapons,
[dwells] on the banks of the Pañcavaṭī.

To the illustrious Padmanābha, who— having entered a vast leaf-hut constructed [by others]— performed the cutting off of Śūrpaṇakhā’s nose, the awakening of Māra, the commencement of the great battle, the yawning, the commissioning of Rāvaṇa, and the destruction of the illusory deer, thereby achieving his purpose.
O night-stalker,

you who were captivated by deception, intent on searching for Sītā, whose wings were weakened by the jolting of the chariot, who liberated Jaṭāyu, and who brought about the death of your dear kinsman— may you depart!
To the illustrious Dāmodara, whose body has its neck, mouth, and belly constricted,
who descended upon the banks of the Pampā river at the instruction of Śabarī,
and who was made beautiful by his conversation with Hanumān and Sugrīva.

Śrī Saṅkarṣaṇa, who brought joy through the delight of Sugrīva’s attainment of sovereignty— following the rending of Vālin after the leaping over Dundubhi’s corpse and the felling of the seven *sāla* trees;
and [the monkeys] Nīla, Jāmbavat, Nala, Kesari, and others, headed by Sugrīva’s own kinsmen.
To the Lord Śrī Vāsudeva, worshipped by the assembly of services of all the leaders of the monkeys; who,
by the power of the ring granted by him,
crossed the ocean of the eloquent and humble speech of Hanumān, and leaped over Laṅkā by surpassing the vital breaths of Rāvaṇa.
The abduction of the daughter of Janaka by the prince who steals the eyes; the burning of the city of Laṅkā;
the establishment [of the lineage]; the slaying of Dīrghabāhu and Duṣṭadyumna; the illustrious Pradyumna;
the foremost among the Podakas.
To the one of great and fierce power for subduing [the wicked], who is worthy of honor and respect, whose own refuge is immeasurable,
who is the source of the arising of merit, the foremost in granting fearlessness to Vibhīṣaṇa, the Unobstructed (Aniruddha)— to the glorious Aniruddha, the boundless.

To the illustrious Puruṣottama, the supreme among all things moving and stationary, who is expert in the liberation [of beings] by means of a bridge capable of performing the consecration for extinguishing the pride of the swelling ocean of salt-water; to Him, the most excellent of all.

Salutations to the glorious Adhokṣaja, who, by the sound of his bowstring— acting as a thunderbolt that shattered the bows of the demons beginning with Nistūla, Prahasta, Kumbhakarṇa, Indrajit, Kumbha, Nikumbha, Agnivarṇa, Atikāya, Mahodara, and Mahāpārśva— dried up their strength and destroyed the entire race of Rākṣasas.
I bow to the glorious Nārasiṃha, whose roar in battle is unimpeded, who brings victory by mauling the necks of the ten-necked Rāvaṇa and the demon Kaṇṭhīrava,
and who dwells in the city of Laṅkā, the abode of the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Bhadra— the younger brother of the Ten-necked One— and known as Dvijākhya.
He who pervades the entire empire, enriched with bliss; the glorious Acyuta;
he whose face is like a blazing fire that causes wonder even to all the gods and demons;
he who is worthy of honor as Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa lean upon his limbs; and he who ascends the magnificent Puṣpaka chariot.

Accompanied by his brothers residing in Nandigrāma, having discarded his matted locks and bark garments, and adorned with ornaments such as the *aphara* [crown], may Śrī Janārdana— who increases our welfare—
[attain] the continuous, great festival of the special coronation (*paṭṭābhiṣeka*) in the city of Ayodhyā that reaches to the ends of the quarters.
O descendant of Bharata,

the assembly hall— white with the six-syllabled mantra— is like a vast ocean of camphor-water with its pearls at rest; it possesses auspicious fame equal to the hundred-fold gifts of a great donor, and resembles the jasmine, the moon, the celestial Ganges, sandalwood, the divine cow, autumnal waters, the finest palm leaves, and the *dampoli* flower.
To Śrī Hari, who is resplendent, whose singular glory pervades all the worlds,
who is dense with the splendor of His glances consecrated for the protection of His devotees,
and who is the source of the twenty-four names beginning with Keśava.
To Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who has accepted his own flute as the wick for the lamp of wisdom,
who is the Brahma-mantra that delivers Pārvatī from the lotus-heart of all the gods, whose every desire is fulfilled, and who is dense with the nectar of the descent of the mountain [Girirāja].

I worship, I worship Rāmabhadra, the auspicious mountain who has severed the fear born of worldly existence, whose heart is a flawless void, who awakens the desires of his devotees, and who is the refuge of Rāmadāsa.
Thus ends the *Cūrṇikā* composed by Śrī Bhadrācalarāmadāsa, which sets forth the twenty-four [deities] beginning with Keśava.
